title: Muru
content:
Muru

Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.

Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.

As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.

Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:

  • 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next
  • 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru
  • 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers
  • 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together
  • 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many
  • 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development
  • 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together
  • 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice
  • 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts
  • 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh
  • 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container
  • 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it
  • 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report
  • 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero
  • 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule
  • 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding
  • 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page
  • 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar

That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

title: To code well, avoid blunders
content:
The secret to writing good code1 is to avoid catastrophic mistakes. Many engineers think about programming as if the goal is to have brilliant insights, but they’re wrong. If you don’t blunder, you will win.

Many other domains are like this. If you can play chess without ever hanging pieces, you will win against almost any2 opponent. If you are very good at returning tennis balls, you will beat most players even if you never hit a winner. People are really bad at internalizing this. They think that being good at chess means finding brilliant tactical combinations, or that being good at tennis means crushing balls into the corner of the court, or that being a good programmer means discovering beautiful new abstractions. Not so! All of those things are valuable, but they are not the main thing. The main thing is to avoid catastrophic mistakes.

The reason programming is like this is that it is impossible to build a durable winning advantage. In basketball, if you are up 99-1, the worst consequence of a blunder is still being up 99-4. However, in programming, one blunder can turn an elegant codebase into a janky one. For instance, consider these blunders:

  • Introducing a parallel system to perform the same task
  • Introducing a second source of truth for some key piece of data
  • Turning a safe sync operation into a delicate async one
  • Adding new subtle points of failure
  • Complicating a key interface

The cardinal sins here are inconsistency and introducing unnecessary requirements3. Even a little bit of inconsistency is dangerous because it breaks trust: instead of assuming your code works the sensible way, engineers must now go looking for surprises.

Unnecessary requirements are dangerous for two reasons. First, they’re sticky. When you’re implementing a new requirement, you have the context to decide whether it’s necessary or not. If you see one in the codebase, you must assume it’s necessary unless you’re willing to spend a bunch of time researching. So requirements tend to remain in codebases long after they could be removed. Second, they often interrelate in dangerous ways: if your codebase supports X, then you must consider how each new feature will interact with X. This combinatorial explosion is what makes working in large codebases so hard4.

When you’re writing code, you must at all costs try to:

  1. Identify where your task could fit most normally into the current codebase
  2. Trim your task down into the smallest set of requirements that you can

In fact, you should be so focused on this — on avoiding blunders — that you don’t really have mental energy to be worrying about cool tricks or “extra credit” features. As with shipping projects, if you find yourself thinking things like “oh, I could implement it with this clever pattern”, this is a warning sign: you are likely becoming distracted from the main thing, and you risk blundering.

You don’t have to be clever to do great programming work. In fact, sometimes cleverness can be a disadvantage. What you need is attention to detail and a laser focus on what actually matters: avoiding blunders by maintaining consistency and skipping unnecessary requirements.

  1. As usual on this blog, I am primarily talking about working on large commercial codebases with big teams: “impure engineering” in my terminology. This advice may not apply if you’re doing other kinds of work. Of course all of this applies whether you’re writing code by hand or driving an AI agent.

    ↩

  2. My guess (it’s surprisingly hard to research) is that not ever blundering would get you around a 1600 or 1700 chess rating: strong enough to win almost every game against casual players.

    ↩

  3. Current coding agents are pretty good at consistency — about as good as humans — but are far worse at avoiding unnecessary requirements, unfortunately.

    ↩

  4. I wrote about this in depth in Wicked features.

    ↩

title: ★ A Week With the New Privacy Controls in MacOS 27.3 Beta 2
content:
On Monday, when the second betas of the v27.3 OSes came out, I posted about Apple adding the new privacy controls they had promised a month prior, in the wake of Meta’s Muse app surprising some users with what information it had access to (e.g., incoming iMessages) after being granted Full Disk Access — which authorization some users just clicked right through. I also posted a link to Apple’s corresponding new support documents. My initial take on Monday:

I’m installing it now, but from what I’ve seen so far, these changes not only alleviate my concerns that Apple might over-tighten the screws, I actually think they add clarity and give users more, not less, control over their Macs.

After a week, I’m willing to call it: this overhaul of these settings and permissions is a win. I really like the way that, for apps asking for Full Disk Access, users can now grant access to a list of folders instead. That’s what I mean about these new settings giving users more control.

Are these new dialog boxes “scarier”? Yes, and the point is, they should be. You should be slightly jolted into attention when an app prompts for any of these permissions. The question is whether they are unnecessarily scary. I would say no, not at all. The descriptions are fair and accurate. Is it unnecessarily scary to show you thumbnails of your personal photos before permitting Full Disk Access that would grant an application unfettered access to your personal photos? No! It’s a bit of a jolt to see them, but that’s just reducing the abstraction. The words “full disk access” feel different than actually seeing a snapshot of what full disk access entails.

Might this discourage some Mac users from granting Full Disk Access to AI agent apps? Yes. And it should! Users who actually understand the stakes will not be dissuaded by these new permissions — when granting them is what they know they want to do. Additionally, I think these new dialog boxes represent very good UI design. They look like a new modern take on MacOS “system chrome” design — not skinny iPhone-sized alerts.

My only gripe about the new stuff is the prominent menu bar indicator that now appears when one app is controlling another. You can’t turn it off (except via an undocumented hidden defaults setting), and it’s distracting on most Macs, and extra distracting on the new MacBook Pros with PROLED displays because on those Macs, it appears in the Dynamic Island! Chance Miller, on Threads (with screenshots):

Most of the changes in macOS 27.3 are reasonable, but this Live Activity thing for system access has got to go. It’s way too aggressive.

It takes over the Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro!

As I write this article on a new MacBook Pro review unit, I have 8 of these indicators in my Dynamic Island: Scroll Reverser, Keyboard Maestro Engine, HazeOver, SteerMouse Manager, Moom, Chest (a promising new utility for managing menu bar icons), System Events, and a new text snippet expansion utility I’m beta testing.

Every one of these apps is running all of the time for me. This indicator being on, all the time, for every one of them isn’t helping me notice unusual activity. If anything, if Apple doesn’t rethink this idea, it’s going to make me miss the indication if an app is taking advantage of access permissions in an unwanted or unexpected way.

Zac Hall, Miller’s colleague at 9to5Mac, published an article on Tuesday showing the command-line defaults incantation to disable this. That’s better than not being able to disable it at all, but I expect Apple to revisit this based on feedback. It seems like a well-intentioned feature that was designed by people who didn’t realize how many always-on utilities “control other apps”.
description: Apple’s new Full Disk Access and other privacy controls in MacOS 27.3 are good, with the exception of the ever-present menu bar indicator for apps that control other apps.

title: Porting Rockbox to an undocumented $9 Aliexpress ‘YP3’ MP3 Player with LLMs
content:
Rockbox is a wonderful old custom firmware project for a variety of MP3 players and iPods. Flashing rockbox to my Sansa E200 was a seminal moment for me: computers were everywhere, and if they didn’t do cool things, it was because no one had bothered to program them to do so. Looking back, that played no small part in my choice of career.

It seems like in 2026 there aren’t any cheap MP3 players that Rockbox supports though. Reverse engineering an embedded platform like this is one of the hardest things I can think of, and I had decided to pay the big bucks for one of those delicious subsidized token plans to try and push it as hard as I could, and I did have a dirt cheap $9 Aliexpress MP3 player lying around.

TL;DR: it ported Rockbox to a 512 KiB player, I was barely involved. Then, I had it build a re-usable toolkit/set of skills for future ports based on what worked from the first attempt approach, and Claude was able to get Rockbox running on another MP3 player (TS47) in 4 hours.

I made a quick website for the project: https://rockslop.jayd.ml

Here is the porting toolkit: auto-rockbox

Enter: The YP3

This is an unbranded player, sold under a variety of fake consonant soup brands on Amazon as well as Aliexpress. You can order them wholesale from Alibaba for less than $7 or so each.

It calls itself a yp3_2.0.43 in the “About” menu as. This appears to be a listing for a YP3 - the original is gone. I paid $9.71 for mine, shipped.

NOTE: Before you run off and buy one, I have another rockbox port that is probably a week or two out, it is booting and stable, just needs more acceptance testing. This device is extremely similar but has 4 MiB PSRAM, so it has fewer compromises

This was $20 on sale

I also have a stack of other random MP3 players I intend to repeat this with

See the project website: https://rockslop.jayd.ml

Special thanks

If anyone gets credit for this rockbox port, it’s ilyakurdyukov - they figured out how to get it into ROM Download mode (Down + USB), and wrote a utility to dump / write flash. Then I could be a little slop kiddie and not have to use a soldering iron.

See the YP3 page on the project website for more info.

The good:

  • It costs $9. If it breaks buy another one.
  • USB-C and Blueooth!
  • There is a physical reset button, device is easily recoverable
  • Unbrickable (if you keep stock bootloader): holding down and resetting brings you into a DFU USB download mode.
  • Someone already figured out how to flash and interact with ROM DFU
  • That ROM DFU mode lets you poke flash and RAM.

The bad

  • SoC: Complete mystery meat Chinese “Smartlink SL6801” / Jointbees. Does not exist online
    • 2x Cortext-M4 r0p1 cpuID 0x410fc241
    • 192 MHz (stock does not vary CPU freq). Has an FPU
    • Capable of Execute In Place (XIP) from flash, but no cache at all. Slow as dirt.
    • When XIP-ing code, cpu1 always waits behind cpu0 and can stall indefinitely if cpu0 is continuously fetching instructions from flash. Very easy to deadlock
  • SRAM 512 KiB plus about ~30 KiB for packets for the bluetooth radio.
  • 2 MB Flash ROM
  • 128x160 full color LCD (RGB565)
  • Only 5 buttons - a dpad with a center press (center press is power & wired to PMU)
  • Bluetooth (with an undocumented stack)

It has 512KiB of SRAM, and the smallest existing Rockbox target was 2 MiB, I was already scrolling Aliexpress for another one, but the LLM said “trust me bro I can make it happen” and I decided to try its luck.

The ugly

  • While the hardware is cheap but functional, stock OS is painful to use
  • It regularly crashes and watchdogs when in USB transfer mode

Where the port ended up

YP3 running Rockbox

After about a week it was booting a build of Rockbox on a crash diet - every single buffer had been cut to the bone, but it could start and play audio. Tuning, bug fixing, etc took another month or so.

I am not aware of anything that isn’t working hardware wise.

The main feature you lose is concurrency while playing music and plugins. Codecs and plugins are already loaded and swapped around at runtime with normal Rockbox, but on this player there is one shared 128 KiB arena for both, so starting a plugin stops music playback.

Other cuts include:

  • No voice
  • Only English is supported
  • DSP: No pitch/speed control, surround, crossfade
  • Cuesheets
  • album art
  • Theme backdrop pictures
  • No dircache, so folders are read straight from SD card
    • Large folders are truncated by default at 256 (configurable from 32 to 512)
  • Playlists are capped at 400
  • Codecs: WMA Pro, Musepack (MPC), RealAudio (Cook), and the chiptune formats SID, NSF, VGM, KSS, HES, SGC, ASAP. WavPack (16-bit), (24-bit/96 kHz)

What made it, somehow:

  • MP3 (up to 320 kbps), AAC/M4A (AAC+ too, HE-AAC v2 plays in mono), WMA, Opus (up to ~192 kbps), Ogg Vorbis, FLAC (stereo, up to 24-bit/96 kHz), ALAC, WAV, AIFF, AU, TTA, APE, Speex, MOD, SPC, AY, GBS, A52/AC3, ATRAC3, Shorten, ADX, VOX, SMAF.

  • The database.

    The database has a new variant that is disk only and has synchronous, blocking updates (ie the player shows a loading screen and stops music when it refreshes and doesn’t refresh in background). I think it also cut the “songs by letter” menu.

    The database requests memory for its menus at runtime, and depending on the size of your theme it can refuse to open the menus.

  • Themes, without backgrounds. load and work, although heavy themes can cause the database to stop opening (handled gracefully with a warning)

  • Bluetooth

    Overnight Claude reverse engineered the bluetooth stack and wrote a bluetooth HAL for Rockbox. I asked it before I went to bed and it was working in the morning.

    No binary blobs are shipped: the bt stack is burned into chip ROM (not flash), and the YP3 bluetooth driver calls into the stack.

A note on codecs

Most of the codecs run from SRAM as normal. MP3, AAC, WMA, Vorbis and Opus, however, wouldn’t fit in our arena nicely, so they run from flash.

But, our XIP flash is dirt slow, so lots of very careful profiling was done to move hot code loops back into SRAM. This kind of profiling had to be done all over Rockbox to get hot loops into SRAM - font rendering, alpha blending, scrolling, etc. This is where most of the “weeks of polishing” went.

Battery Life

Largely comparable to stock. I hooked the player up to the PC’s line in or fake bluetooth sink and set it to repeat Daft Punks Random Access Memories. A script on the PC detected when it cut out.

Stock: 21.29 hours wired, 20.07 on Bluetooth

Rockbox: 20.07 hours wired, 19.3 on Bluetooth

There was some variation in the battery voltage at start, and this was just one run, so expect some variation.

Battery life is surprisingly impressive on this player,

Approach

I’m one of those software guys, I can’t solder or find UART pads to save my life. This was an entirely software only port; I haven’t ever opened mine up.

I hooked up ghidra-mcp and let it start pulling the firmware apart. It figured out how to inject tasks into the running RTOS (FreeRTOS) in bootloader mode. This allowed it to probe the hardware and even write drivers before attempting a Rockbox boot.

To be clear: this is 100% vibecoded. I have only glanced at some of the code it wrote. I contributed my approach to development and testing, was the PM and QA person, and the agent’s little meat robot to reboot it when it crashed or wander around my house with headphones on while it tuned the bluetooth radio. I haven’t doneC and firmware development for years.

Cleanroom

Initially I let the same agent do the reverse engineering as implementation. Later I had it go through and rip out anything that wasn’t a hardware fact (ie a register) and re-did the drivers with a cleanroom setup. One dirty agent with Ghidra, one referee agent in between to make sure nothing leaks, and the implementation agent. Subsequent ports used a variation of this setup from the beginning

The most work I have done personally on this project is writing this blog post.

Robotic eyes and ears

  • Webcam pointed at the screen, so the model could see what the player was doing and to work on the LCD drivers.

  • Webcam mic for bringing up the speaker

    (had to yell at Claude when it decided to start playing tones at 2 AM)

  • Headphone jack plugged into Line In on my PC (finally, I used it!!)

    This allowed it to test and tune audio output.

  • Bluetooth adapter. I plugged in a bluetooth adapter and gave it full reign for testing. It used Google’s Bumble python bluetooth stack to have the PC pretend to be headphones
  • Claude kept picking “We Will Rock You” as a test track. I choose to believe this is evidence of a subtle sense of humor when working on a Rockbox port

Opus 5.5 »»»> Sol

This port was started with Codex/Sol 5.6. It was making progress, but was incredibly risk averse and slow. It took it 5 days or so and dozens of manual resets on my part until it felt ready to flash something and boot it.

I should have told it how to figure out how to arm the watchdog and reboot into download mode itself sooner. Codex got it to showing the rockbox logo with buggy drivers stubbed out, but had clearly lost its mind in the meantime. I hadn’t been paying attention too closely, but as it had spun around it had:

  • Created 55 GB of files in 2,567 dirs. 3.87 million files total
  • 443 one off tool scripts, 384 documents written
  • an incredibly paranoid flasher that would check each block as it was written and took 15 minutes to write 2 MiB

    • This flashing script - and many other tool scripts - would check the sha256 of the documentation files they depended on to ensure nothing had changed.

      It’s kind of beautiful in its own insane way: this seems to be an attempt to work around multiple agents and memory limits. Madness though

  • An MCP server with tons of ceremony and tools around flashing things, running tests, etc

Claude immediately threw that garbage away and wrote like a few python scripts to use instead. Auto mode in claude code helped too.

The subsequent TS17 port went from me plugging it in to a usable alpha build in about 4 hours with Opus 5.5 (there was little to re-use from the YP3 other than scripts and skills).

Bidirectional Rockbox Dev Shell

This is one of the most valuable things it did. Rockbox has an existing one-way USB serial driver for logs. I had that extended to have dozens of little commands to drive the player, everything from injecting keypresses to taking screenshots to debugging the bluetooth radio.

This was critical for completely hands off development - I had it build a torture test suite in Python that would monkey-test the player for hours, pressing buttons at random. Many bugs were found doing this - including some in Rockbox upstream. At this point the player has hundreds of hours of bench testing under Rockbox - I could just leave it running and Claude would patiently watch the test logs for new failures to diagnose and fix.

An agent can reboot to recovery, flash firmware, reboot into Rockbox, run tests, see what is on the screen, hear what it is doing, completely on its own. Most of the development of this project happened while I was asleep.

Audio Tuning

For audio (and battery endurance testing) Claude had me set up a 3.5 mm splitter with one end going into the PC’s Line In and the other going into real headphones to provide an actual load.

Then I had it build a test suite and file that plays a variety of sweeps and test tones. I used an Apple lightning adapter to use as the ground truth for this setup, then used it to compare audio levels and frequency response.

My PC’s sound card is not high sensitivity equipment, but this is enough of a sanity check for me.

More charts that I don’t understand</summary> </details>

The Hardest Parts

There were two tricky things to work out that Claude struggled to fix. The exact power off sequence took quite a few tries, probably because it was the only thing I had to be there to test, it couldn’t just work on it for hours overnight.

The other crazy bug was that the FM radio sounded terrible. You could tune to a station, but the sound was distorted and clipped. Claude spent forever trying to figure out why, but eventually I noticed that the frequency it was tuned to did not match the station identifier over the air.

It turns out the tuner had been set up with a slightly wrong clock source, so it was ~4 MhZ off. It just so happened to work out that when I tuned it to my test station, it could kind of lock on to another one, but sounded terrible.

Other New Features

Plugin Psychosis

I told Claude to port as many games as it could to Rockbox.

This release adds THREE HUNDRED AND FIFTY SEVEN new plugins. That is not a typo: 357. Most of these are ports, a few are originals. Given the quantity here I haven’t done enough QA here.

Originals

RockGPT

This is going to get its own blog post because it is deeply amusing. A ~1 million param model running on your MP3 player. Almost coherent, fine tuned to be aloof and dismissive of humanity. Weights are streamed from SD card. Crazy

RockTrack

A little tracker/chiptune editor for Rockbox. I haven’t had a ton of time to test this one. Probably needs ergonomic improvements.

Video Player

Rockbox’s existing mpegplayer didn’t fit on the YP3 and I didn’t want to hack it up too much, so I had Claude write a new one, with a nicer pixel art UI, MKV support. AVI, MKV, MP4; MPEG-1/2, MJPEG.

Ports

There are too many to list. Here is the full set of ports

  • Anarch - FOSS DOOM clone
  • Celeste Classic - Platformer Maddy Thorson, Noel Berry
  • MicroCity City builder, jhhoward
  • Prizm Racing, Racing, duarteapcoelho
  • Rockcraft Minecraft-style block sandbox, port of Blocks-TI-84 by The Science Elf, MIT
  • Terrario, Terraria-like KBD2
  • Jet Island, 3D island demo CubeCoders
  • Rock88, 3D rendered Film player demo JetExamples

Bulk Ports

We got to stupid plugin numbers by writing compat shims/libraries for several popular open source players:

  • Arduboy: 240
  • Pokitto: 23
  • Flipper Zero: 33
  • Gamebuino: 17

Misc Features

  • Enhanced RDS: program type names, call letters, clock time, RadioText+ (artist/title)
  • Charge limiter (hardware dependent, allows 50-100% cap)

  • Bluetooth HID drivers

    Yes, you can pair a PS4 controller or keyboard to Rockbox. I wanted to see how much we could do with the existing Bluetooth stack

  • Bluetooth headset battery level detection, with an icon in the status bar

Themes

I had it port some themes from the Rockbox website to work on this screensize, add a bluetooth status icon, and it generated 5 original themes: Ukiyo (my favorite), Asterism, Chaldani, Lavenia, Cyanotype.

Note: This is a WIP screenshot, there have been bug fixes & some of these got cut because of unclear licensing.

Note that heavy themes can cause some issues, so I would suggest sticking with lightweight ones.

Fin

Well, reverse engineering a completely undocumented chipset was one of the hardest things I could think of to do, and Claude can ace it. I’m planning on porting Rockbox to a bunch of other cheap MP3 players.

THEY ALL SHALL RUN ROCKBOX!

Appendix: Identifying a YP3

There are lots of clones that look like each other. The YP3 specifically:

  • Only has 5 buttons - dpad and center
    • no power, volume
    • symbols molded into buttons, not printed on them in white
  • Has a reset pinhole on the right
  • Speaker on top rear
  • USB on bottom right, headphone jack on left
  • SD card on the left
  • I think they’re all black

Also, these screens are made of cheese, you’ll want a screen protector.

title: Weekly Update 531: Optimizely. Script Dependencies & Third Parties
content: "You can't outsource accountability". But it feels like that's what's happening when a disclosure notice refers to "an incident being at a third party", as though somehow that makes it better. It feels like the intent is to deflect responsibility, but ultimately, accountability remains with the party we entrusted our data to in the first place. It's also ultimately them who needs to decide whether to disclose the incident, so in the case of Optimizely this week, even though it's clearly their fault, it's up to the likes of Norwegian Airlines to decide whether they're contacting impacted individuals. And then, in their case, they haven't named the third party anyway! Strange times, I reckon.
